ocar.opportunity: Connectomes and other graphs are inferred from imperfect edge evidence, so statistical tasks such as labeling neurons should account for that observation error rather than treating the reconstructed graph as ground truth.
ocar.challenge: More informative edge features cost more, so one cannot assess every possible edge at high quality; the quantity/quality operating point for the intermediate edge-classification step is usually chosen ad hoc rather than to maximize the downstream inference task.
ocar.action: Priebe, Sussman, Tang, and Vogelstein (arXiv 2014; later Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics) formulate errorfully observed graphs in a stochastic blockmodel, derive an optimal quantity/quality operating point for a simple but optimal vertex classifier, and apply the trade-off to errorful observations of the C. elegans connectome.
ocar.resolution: Optimal operating points are surprising: methods for the intermediate edge task should be chosen to maximize subsequent vertex classification, not edge accuracy itself. The C. elegans connectome is used as a scientific case of this quantity/quality trade-off.
ocar.future_work: The extract’s later sections analogize the same trade-off to social-network topic modeling (e.g., Enron email) and do not report a numeric C. elegans accuracy table in the selected text.

summaries.beginner: Wiring maps are built from noisy guesses about which cells touch. This paper asks how carefully you should check each possible connection if the real goal is to label the cells, not to get every edge perfect.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2014 arXiv manuscript later published in JCGS, Priebe, Sussman, Tang, and Vogelstein treat graphs whose edges are classified from noisy “edge features.” The downstream task is vertex classification in a stochastic blockmodel. They derive an optimal quantity/quality operating point and argue that intermediate edge methods should be chosen to maximize that later inference. The C. elegans connectome is the scientific example; social-network topic modeling is discussed as a parallel trade-off.
summaries.advanced: The selected extract is the matching Priebe et al. paper (title and authors align). No numeric C. elegans classification rates or explicit τ/κ operating-point values appear in the selected front matter and discussion fragments. The “surprising” operating points are asserted rather than tabulated here. Catalog year is 2012; the extract is arXiv v4 dated 21 Jul 2014.

plain_language_summary: Wiring maps are built from noisy guesses about which cells touch. This paper asks how carefully you should check each possible connection if the real goal is to label the cells, not to get every edge perfect.

ocar.opportunity: Understanding brain function requires integrating vast, heterogeneous data across scales; neuroinformatics could accelerate that synthesis if sharing, ontologies, and mining tools became routine.
ocar.challenge: Neuroscience still generated diverse experimental data faster than they could be capitalized on, and connectomics plus community databases were nascent rather than a working culture of machine-first data use.
ocar.action: Akil, Martone, and Van Essen, in Science (2011), review the need for neuroinformatics using connectomics (macroscopic pathways versus microscopic synapses) and the Neuroscience Information Framework (NIF) as illustrative examples.
ocar.resolution: They argue that mining across multiple tiers of neuroscience information will not fulfill its potential without cultural and infrastructure changes, and they list concrete practices: community ontologies and identifiers, standardized tables for published coordinates, investment in computational synthesis, education in data mining, and cultural participation in sharing.
ocar.future_work: The piece is a program for the field, not a new dataset; Human Connectome Project and NIF funding are acknowledged as the institutional vehicles rather than results demonstrated here.

summaries.beginner: Brain research produces huge piles of different kinds of data. This Science essay argues that sharing, standard labels, and computer-readable tables are needed if anyone is going to put those piles together.
summaries.intermediate: In Science (2011), Akil, Martone, and Van Essen frame neuroinformatics around “neural choreography” and two examples: nascent connectomics at macroscopic versus microscopic scales, and the Neuroscience Information Framework spanning many database types. They quote order-of-magnitude human-brain figures (~80 billion neurons, ~150 trillion synapses) and close with numbered recommendations on ontologies, standardized neuroimaging tables, machine-first consumption of papers, education, and cultural change.
summaries.advanced: This is a perspective, not an empirical map. Neuron and synapse counts are cited from prior work. Connectomics is described as nascent. The extract’s discussion is a list of community practices rather than a quantitative evaluation of NIF or of any particular connectome project.

plain_language_summary: Brain research produces huge piles of different kinds of data. This Science essay argues that sharing, standard labels, and computer-readable tables are needed if anyone is going to put those piles together.

ocar.opportunity: A searchable map of anatomical connections among rat retrosplenial cortex and hippocampal–parahippocampal regions would help interpret overlapping roles in memory, navigation, and prospective thinking.
ocar.challenge: The exact role of retrosplenial cortex and functional differences among its subdivisions remained elusive, and prior interactive accounts had covered hippocampal–parahippocampal networks without a full RSC add-on.
ocar.action: Sugar, Witter, van Strien, and Cappaert, in Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2011), compile anterograde and retrograde tracing literature into an interactive, searchable connectome of rat RSC intrinsic connectivity and RSC–HF–PHR connections, extending their earlier hippocampal–parahippocampal account.
ocar.resolution: The database is described as 223 references in 710 records covering approximately 2600 connections, with RSC subdivided into A29a, A29b, A29c, and A30 (Vogt et al. 2004). Independent retrograde and anterograde results were combined so layers of origin and termination could be assigned, and a search dialog was added relative to the prior version.
ocar.future_work: The resource is a literature synthesis meant to help define RSC function; it does not itself resolve subdivision-specific cognition or human homology.

summaries.beginner: Researchers gathered published tracing studies of a memory-and-navigation region in the rat and turned them into a searchable wiring map, including how that region talks to the hippocampus.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2011), Sugar, Witter, van Strien, and Cappaert extend a prior rat hippocampal–parahippocampal interactive connectome with retrosplenial cortex (RSC) intrinsic connections and RSC–HF–PHR links. Tracing reports were verified by at least two authors, combined for origin and termination layers, and drawn into a searchable PDF. The database is stated as 223 references, 710 records, and about 2600 connections, with RSC divided into A29a–c and A30.
summaries.advanced: This is a collated tracing literature map, not new experiments. Connection totals are literature-derived. Subdivision follows Vogt et al. (2004); other nomenclatures are tabulated. Human default-mode overlap is cited as motivation, not a human connectome result. Accuracy depends on the underlying tracing papers.

plain_language_summary: Researchers gathered published tracing studies of a memory-and-navigation region in the rat and turned them into a searchable wiring map, including how that region talks to the hippocampus.

ocar.opportunity: Linking a neuron’s physiology to its genes and its presynaptic partners in the intact brain would let systems neuroscience combine biophysics with circuit anatomy in the same cell.
ocar.challenge: Existing gene-delivery methods did not allow electrophysiological characterization of the same cell that would later be genetically manipulated.
ocar.action: Rancz, Franks, Schwarz, Pichler, Schaefer, and Margrie, in Nature Neuroscience (2011), show in mouse brain in vivo that neurons survive ‘blind’ whole-cell recording, that DNA can be delivered through the patch pipette, and that plasmids drive expression for at least seven days, illustrated by recording visually evoked synaptic responses in primary visual cortex while delivering plasmids for retrograde monosynaptic tracing of that cell’s inputs.
ocar.resolution: They report high post-recording survival (morphological criteria up to 51 hours) and that the likelihood of genetic manipulation is relatively high (~50%). Recorded cells continued to express reporters for up to a week and could withstand subsequent viral infection. Multiple reporter plasmids (up to three) co-expressed when recovered. Series resistance is identified as the main factor affecting recovery of biocytin-filled and DNA-loaded cells.
ocar.future_work: The discussion lists applications from perturbing signaling cascades to expressing indicators across functionally related presynaptic circuits, and notes that an upper limit on plasmid number was not established.

summaries.beginner: The team records from a living mouse neuron through a tiny pipette, then uses that same pipette to insert DNA so the cell can later be genetically labeled and its input partners traced.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Neuroscience (2011), Rancz and colleagues demonstrate in vivo whole-cell transfection in mouse. Neurons remain intact after blind patching; DNA vectors delivered via the pipette drive protein expression for at least seven days. They illustrate the method by recording visually evoked synaptic responses in V1 while delivering plasmids for retrograde monosynaptic tracing, claiming the first combined synaptic and anatomical receptive field of a neuron. Discussion emphasizes ~50% genetic-manipulation likelihood, week-long reporter expression, and series resistance as the key recovery factor.
summaries.advanced: “First” synaptic-plus-anatomical receptive field is an authorship claim. Survival was scored morphologically, not with long-term physiology in the discussion excerpt. Quantitative tracing completeness and numbers of reconstructed presynaptic partners are not in the selected extract. Applications beyond the V1 illustration are proposed.

plain_language_summary: The team records from a living mouse neuron through a tiny pipette, then uses that same pipette to insert DNA so the cell can later be genetically labeled and its input partners traced.

ocar.opportunity: Spinal reflex circuits are a prototypic CNS system in which to find recognition molecules that set fine synaptic specificity between proprioceptive sensory neurons and motor pools.
ocar.challenge: Monosynaptic sensory–motor connections are initially accurate without activity, implying surface matching, but determinants of that fine specificity were undefined, as in most CNS circuits.
ocar.action: Pecho-Vrieseling, Sigrist, Yoshida, Jessell, and Arber, in Nature (2009), genetically manipulate Sema3e in selected motor pools and its high-affinity receptor PlexinD1 in proprioceptive sensory neurons in mice, combining physiology, retrograde tracing from cutaneous maximus and triceps, immunohistochemistry, and in situ hybridization.
ocar.resolution: Changing Sema3e–PlexinD1 signaling rewires monosynaptic connections functionally and anatomically but does not alter motor-pool specificity. The authors conclude that this prototypic circuit is constructed through a recognition program based on repellent signaling.
ocar.future_work: How this repellent matching interacts with other recognition systems that do set pool identity is left as the broader specificity problem; the extract’s methods describe p5–p7 recordings and p12–p14 tracing rather than adult behavior.

summaries.beginner: Some spinal sensory neurons should wire only to particular motor neurons. This mouse study finds a molecular “keep away” signal that sets those fine connections without changing which muscle each motor pool belongs to.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2009), Pecho-Vrieseling and colleagues show that Sema3e on selected motor pools and PlexinD1 on proprioceptive afferents are a critical recognition pair in mouse sensory–motor reflex circuits. Genetic changes in either partner rewire monosynaptic connections but spare motor-pool specificity, supporting a repellent matching program. Physiology (p5–p7) and retrograde tracing from cutaneous maximus and triceps (p12–p14) with vGlut1 quantification are the main assays named in the extract.
summaries.advanced: Motor-pool specificity is reported as unchanged; the rewiring claim is qualitative in this extract (no percent connectivity tables). Sema3e is motivated partly by Pea3 mutants. The study addresses brachial circuits in neonatal mice, not a whole-CNS wiring code. Catalog organism tags are empty; the paper is mouse genetics.

plain_language_summary: Some spinal sensory neurons should wire only to particular motor neurons. This mouse study finds a molecular “keep away” signal that sets those fine connections without changing which muscle each motor pool belongs to.

ocar.opportunity: Intrinsically photosensitive melanopsin ganglion cells sit in retinal circuits fed by rods and cones, so mapping their morphology and synapses would clarify how irradiance signals are combined with image-forming input.
ocar.challenge: That circuitry was poorly understood, including whether inner- and outer-stratifying melanopsin cells are independent populations and what bipolar versus amacrine input they receive.
ocar.action: Jusuf, Lee, Hannibal, and Grünert, in the European Journal of Neuroscience (2007), as described in the catalog abstract, study melanopsin-containing ganglion cells in common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus) with morphology, tiling, and synaptic markers (CtBP2 for presumed bipolar synapses; gephyrin for presumed amacrine synapses).
ocar.resolution: Outer-stratifying dendrites tile with little overlap, whereas they largely overlap inner-stratifying fields, suggesting independent populations. Both types show colocalized puncta for both markers across the dendritic tree. CtBP2 density on inner dendrites was about 50% higher than on outer dendrites; gephyrin density was comparable between strata but higher than CtBP2. Inner-stratifying cells may receive input from diffuse bipolar DB6.
ocar.future_work: The abstract frames the pattern as consistent with bipolar and amacrine input across the tree; it does not report functional recordings.

summaries.beginner: Some primate retinal cells contain the pigment melanopsin and also receive ordinary photoreceptor input. This study maps those cells in marmoset and counts likely synapses on their inner versus outer dendrites.
summaries.intermediate: In the European Journal of Neuroscience (2007), Jusuf, Lee, Hannibal, and Grünert characterize melanopsin ganglion cells in marmoset. Outer-stratifying cells tile; inner- and outer-stratifying fields overlap. Using CtBP2 and gephyrin puncta, both populations appear to receive bipolar and amacrine input across the dendritic tree, with CtBP2 density about 50% higher on inner dendrites. Inner-stratifying cells are suggested to receive DB6 bipolar input.
summaries.advanced: The attached PDF extract does not match this catalog record: it is Baakdhah and Sivak, In vitro retinal ganglion cell differentiation and enrichment (Front. Cell Dev. Biol., 2026), not Jusuf et al. 2007 on marmoset melanopsin cells. Summaries here follow the EJN abstract only. No tiling statistics beyond the qualitative overlap claim, and no absolute puncta densities, appear in that abstract.

plain_language_summary: Some primate retinal cells contain the pigment melanopsin and also receive ordinary photoreceptor input. This study maps those cells in marmoset and counts likely synapses on their inner versus outer dendrites.

ocar.opportunity: If genetic and lifestyle Alzheimer’s risk factors leave fingerprints on brain networks before amyloid/tau pathology, those circuits could become translational biomarkers and intervention targets.
ocar.challenge: APOE, age, sex, diet, and immunity are entangled, so unique and shared network effects are hard to separate in humans, especially without disease pathology as a confounder.
ocar.action: Winter, Mahzarnia, Anderson, Han, Tremblay, Stout, Moon, Marcellino, Dunson, and Badea, in Magnetic Resonance Imaging (2024), use mice expressing human APOE and NOS2 (reduced innate immune response versus mouse Nos2) and apply network topology plus GraphClass, and sparse CCA including spatial memory, to accelerated diffusion-MRI connectomes in a cross-sectional multi-risk design without AD pathology.
ocar.resolution: Risk factors converged on a circuit of 63 of 54,946 connections (0.11% of the connectome). Sparse CCA with spatial memory yielded 80 edges overlapping diet (47), immunity (39), APOE3 vs 4 (26), sex (23), and age (19). Discussion reports APOE3 versus APOE4 as the largest genotype contrast (1.4% of edges), then APOE2 vs 3 (0.5%) and APOE2 vs 4 (0.4%), and the largest networks for diet (1626 edges) versus age (~300). APOE2 connectomes were more similar to APOE4 than expected from risk labels.
ocar.future_work: The authors position the fingerprints for distinguishing high- versus low-risk participants at preclinical stages and for designing APOE-genotype-specific immune interventions; human translation is implied, not demonstrated here.

summaries.beginner: Mice carrying human Alzheimer’s risk genes, but not plaques, still show distinctive brain-network patterns for diet, sex, immunity, and APOE type. A small shared bundle of connections is hit by several of those risks at once.
summaries.intermediate: In Magnetic Resonance Imaging (2024), Winter, Mahzarnia, Badea and colleagues analyze diffusion-MRI connectomes from humanized APOE/NOS2 mice without AD pathology. GraphClass and topology isolate networks for age, high-fat diet, sex, APOE, and immunity; 63/54,946 edges (0.11%) are shared. Sparse CCA with spatial memory finds an 80-edge network overlapping those risk graphs. Discussion highlights a 1.4% APOE3-versus-APOE4 edge difference and far more diet- than age-affected edges (1626 vs ~300).
summaries.advanced: This is a mouse diffusion connectome without AD histopathology, not a human clinical test. The 0.11% shared circuit is a GraphClass overlap, not a proven causal bottleneck. APOE2 similarity to APOE4 is reported as surprising and tied to navigation-strategy citations. Imaging is accelerated DWI; synaptic-resolution claims are not made.

plain_language_summary: Mice carrying human Alzheimer’s risk genes, but not plaques, still show distinctive brain-network patterns for diet, sex, immunity, and APOE type. A small shared bundle of connections is hit by several of those risks at once.

ocar.opportunity: A genetically tractable critical-period circuit in Drosophila can show how early sensory experience recruits glia to prune specific synaptic glomeruli.
ocar.challenge: Experience can expand or retract different olfactory sensory neuron classes, but the glial receptor-to-cytoskeleton sequence for temporally restricted pruning was not defined.
ocar.action: Nelson, Vita, and Broadie, in Scientific Reports (2024), combine mutants, transgenic RNAi, and glia-targeted expression in the juvenile fly olfactory system, focusing on ethyl-butyrate-responsive Or42a neurons innervating VM7 after 24-hour critical-period exposure from 0–1 day post-eclosion.
ocar.resolution: They report a sequential pathway: experience drives glial infiltration of neuropil; Draper/MEGF10 receptors engage antagonistic Basket/JNK and Puckered/DUSP signaling for nuclear translocation of activated Basket; Cheerio/FLNA is induced and is described as absolutely essential for glomeruli pruning via glial F-actin remodeling. Glial cheerio RNAi abolishes VM7 pruning after odorant experience in the quantified figure described in the extract.
ocar.future_work: Other OSN classes that expand rather than retract with experience are cited as a contrast; whether the same Draper–JNK–Cheerio cassette generalizes to those classes is not established here.

summaries.beginner: In young fruit flies, a burst of odor experience makes support cells eat away part of a smell circuit. The authors trace the molecular steps inside those glial cells that carry out the pruning.
summaries.intermediate: In Scientific Reports (2024), Nelson, Vita, and Broadie show that glia prune Drosophila Or42a→VM7 synaptic glomeruli after critical-period ethyl butyrate (24 h, 0–1 dpe). Draper (MEGF10) is required; Basket (JNK) versus Puckered (DUSP) control nuclear translocation of activated Basket; Cheerio (FLNA) is required for F-actin remodeling and pruning. Figure 7 in the extract reports complete failure of experience-dependent VM7 pruning with glial cheerio RNAi (p ≤ 0.0001 versus control; NS for other comparisons as plotted).
summaries.advanced: The pathway is worked out in one glomerulus/OSN class (Or42a/VM7) during a defined 0–1 dpe window. “Absolutely essential” refers to Cheerio in this assay. Other OSN classes can expand with experience; that opposite plasticity is cited, not mapped onto Cheerio. Exact innervation-volume means are plotted but not typed as numbers in the selected text besides the p-value flags.

plain_language_summary: In young fruit flies, a burst of odor experience makes support cells eat away part of a smell circuit. The authors trace the molecular steps inside those glial cells that carry out the pruning.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-nervous-system single-cell transcriptomes from related nematodes could reveal which features of neuronal identity and signaling are conserved versus evolvable over tens of millions of years.
ocar.challenge: Comparative work often samples a few cell types; whether novel neuron classes arise, and whether transmitters, receptors, or neuropeptides move independently, was unknown at nervous-system scale.
ocar.action: Toker, Ripoll-Sánchez, Geiger, Saini, Beets, Vértes, Schafer, Ben-David, and Hobert, on bioRxiv (2024), generate whole-animal single-cell transcriptomes of three Caenorhabditis species and compare neuronal identities, neurotransmitter pathways, and neuropeptidergic networks.
ocar.resolution: Neuronal cell-type identities were stable over more than 45 million years, with combinatorial homeodomain transcription factors among the best classifiers of homologous classes; no novel neuronal cell types were found. Neurotransmitter-producing identities remain stable, but ionotropic and metabotropic receptors diverge so that more than half of neuron classes change their capacity to receive specific transmitters. Neuropeptides and receptors are divergent while wireless neuropeptide-network topology stays dense and stable. Small secreted proteins lacking conventional neuropeptide hallmarks show similarly cell-type-specific, evolvable expression. Sensory neurons diverge faster in non-conserved genes; motor neurons are unusually stable in orthologous-gene expression.
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest homeobox combinations may help classify neurons in animals with less transcription-factor genetics; whether receptor divergence is the main source of circuit novelty remains an interpretive claim.

summaries.beginner: Three worm species kept the same neuron types for tens of millions of years, but many cells changed which chemical messages they can hear. Identity stayed put; the listening equipment evolved.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2024), Toker, Hobert and colleagues compare whole-animal single-cell transcriptomes across three Caenorhabditis species diverged more than 45 million years. Homologous neuron classes match, especially via homeodomain combinations, with no novel classes. Transmitter-producing cells are stable, but receptors for ACh, GABA, glutamate, and monoamines are plastic in more than half of classes. Neuropeptidergic connectome topology remains dense despite ligand/receptor turnover. Discussion adds faster non-conserved-gene change in sensory neurons and unusual ortholog stability in motor neurons.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint. Divergence times (>40 vs >45 million years) are stated at two precisions. Receptor “capacity” is inferred from expression, not physiology. The wireless neuropeptide connectome’s “stable dense topology” is a graph-level claim without numeric edge-overlap in this extract. Novel secreted proteins are candidates, not proven transmitters.

plain_language_summary: Three worm species kept the same neuron types for tens of millions of years, but many cells changed which chemical messages they can hear. Identity stayed put; the listening equipment evolved.

ocar.opportunity: Monosynaptic rabies tracing is a workhorse of mesoscale circuit mapping; adding reporters that work from fluorescence through electron microscopy would link the same labeled neurons across scales in health and disease models.
ocar.challenge: Existing ΔG rabies variants were not designed as a coordinated kit for subcellular targeting, calcium imaging, automated counting, and correlative EM in the same resource set.
ocar.action: Bouin, Wu, Koyuncu, Ye, Kim, Wu, Tong, Chen, Phan, Mackey, Ramachandra, Ellisman, Holmes, Semler, and Xu, in Molecular Psychiatry (2024), report 20 new recombinant rabies vectors for multi-scale, multi-modal mapping, including improved fluorescent proteins, subcellular targeting, calcium indicators, and GFP plus ferritin for dual fluorescence and EM.
ocar.resolution: They demonstrate microstructural changes in rabies-labeled neurons in aging and Alzheimer’s mouse models, live calcium imaging, automated measurement of infected neurons, and dual EM/mesoscale imaging with GFP–ferritin reporters. The paper is presented as expanding the scale and power of RV-mediated labeling across imaging scales.
ocar.future_work: The selected extract’s discussion was not captured (the text jumps from the introduction to author contributions), so limitations, cytotoxicity, and completeness of transsynaptic restriction are not evaluated from discussion text here.

summaries.beginner: Rabies viruses can jump one synapse so scientists can see which cells talk to which. This team built twenty new versions that glow better, mark tiny parts of cells, or show up in both light and electron microscopes.
summaries.intermediate: In Molecular Psychiatry (2024), Bouin, Xu and colleagues introduce 20 recombinant rabies virus vectors for multi-scale circuit mapping. Tools include improved fluorescent proteins, subcellular targeting, calcium indicators, automated counting of infected neurons, and GFP plus ferritin for correlative fluorescence and EM. Applications named in the abstract include aging and Alzheimer’s mouse models. The introduction reviews G-deleted, trans-complemented, and pseudotyped RV systems as the platform being extended.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF text does not include a results or discussion section (it runs from abstract/introduction into author contributions). Quantitative infection rates, toxicity, and EM resolution claims are therefore taken from the abstract only. “20 new” is the resource count; per-vector performance tables are not in this extract. Catalog method tag includes electron microscopy, matching the GFP–ferritin demonstration claim.

plain_language_summary: Rabies viruses can jump one synapse so scientists can see which cells talk to which. This team built twenty new versions that glow better, mark tiny parts of cells, or show up in both light and electron microscopes.

ocar.opportunity: If skull-constrained wiring cost scales with brain size, comparative mammalian connectomes could show how modularity and communication policy change as volume grows over orders of magnitude.
ocar.challenge: Most network studies cannot hold reconstruction methods fixed across a wide volume range, so volume–topology relations are confounded by species sampling and acquisition differences.
ocar.action: Puxeddu, Faskowitz, Seguin, Yovel, Assaf, Betzel, and Sporns, in PLoS Biology (2024), analyze the MaMI diffusion-MRI database of mammalian connectomes from 201 animals covering 103 species and 12 taxonomic orders, with brain size spanning more than four orders of magnitude, focusing on multiresolution modules and communication.
ocar.resolution: As volume increases, modules become more spatially compact and dense and comprise more costly connections; node distance increasingly impacts communication efficiency. Smaller brains are more efficient under routing-like signaling and larger brains under diffusion-like signaling. In larger brains, modular structure imposes stronger constraints on network signaling. Altogether, spatial embedding is argued to restrict larger brains more tightly.
ocar.future_work: Methods note that bore limits forced 7 T versus 3 T protocols for small versus large brains (approximately <0.15 ml vs >1,000 ml), so scanner differences remain a caveat for volume effects.

summaries.beginner: Bigger mammal brains are not just scaled-up small ones. This study of more than a hundred species finds that large brains pack modules more tightly and rely more on spreading signals than on shortest-path routing.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Biology (2024), Puxeddu, Sporns and colleagues relate connectome topology to brain volume in the MaMI set: 201 animals, 103 species, 12 orders, volume spanning more than four orders of magnitude. Multiresolution modules become more compact, dense, and costly with volume. Communication analyses associate small brains with routing efficiency and large brains with diffusion-like signaling, with modules constraining signaling more in larger brains. Brains were ex vivo DWI; small brains ~<0.15 ml at 7 T and large brains ~>1,000 ml at 3 T.
summaries.advanced: Abstract N (201 animals / 103 species) differs slightly from the methods fragment (225 mammals / 125 species); use the abstract figures for the analyzed claim. 7 T versus 3 T acquisition is an acknowledged hardware split. Connectomes are diffusion tractography, not synaptic maps. Routing versus diffusion “policies” are modeling interpretations of communication efficiency, not measured spike flow.

plain_language_summary: Bigger mammal brains are not just scaled-up small ones. This study of more than a hundred species finds that large brains pack modules more tightly and rely more on spreading signals than on shortest-path routing.

ocar.opportunity: Choosing the right mouse model for a given Alzheimer’s question requires matching pathology, behavior, sex effects, and molecular signatures to human disease rather than defaulting to classic overexpression lines.
ocar.challenge: Traditional transgenic overexpression of familial-AD mutations can misrepresent proteinopathy; knock-in/knock-out and CRISPR models for familial and sporadic risk genes exist but are hard to compare systematically.
ocar.action: Zhong, Peng, Lemos Duarte, Wang, and Cai, in Molecular Neurodegeneration (2024), review commonly used and newer AD mouse models, covering amyloid and tau pathology, synaptic and neuronal degeneration, cognitive and behavioral deficits, sex-specific features, and omics signatures versus human AD brain changes.
ocar.resolution: The review is organized to guide selection of models for specific research questions by cataloging presence or absence of key AD features and limitations of overexpression versus gene-edited lines.
ocar.future_work: The authors hope omics categorization will improve future model choice; the selected extract does not include the comparison tables themselves.

summaries.beginner: Not every Alzheimer’s mouse is the same. This review compares older overexpression lines with newer gene-edited models so labs can pick an animal that actually matches the question they want to ask.
summaries.intermediate: In Molecular Neurodegeneration (2024), Zhong, Peng, Lemos Duarte, Wang, and Cai review transgenic overexpression models of familial AD mutations and newer KI/KO or CRISPR models for familial and sporadic risk genes. They summarize amyloid and tau pathology, degeneration, behavior, sex-specific features, and omics signatures intended to resemble human AD brain changes, with the stated goal of guiding model selection.
summaries.advanced: The selected extract is mostly the abstract, a short introduction, and end-matter; phenotype tables and omics figures are not in the selected text. This is a review, not new mouse data. Healthcare-cost and ranking statistics in the introduction are background, not model results. Catalog axis is health_translation; synaptic/connectomic phenotypes are discussed as model features, not a new connectome.

plain_language_summary: Not every Alzheimer’s mouse is the same. This review compares older overexpression lines with newer gene-edited models so labs can pick an animal that actually matches the question they want to ask.

ocar.opportunity: If oncologists could forecast both how a diffuse low-grade glioma will evolve and how that patient’s connectome will reorganize, they could sequence surgery and adjuvant therapy one step ahead of malignant transformation while protecting cognition.
ocar.challenge: LGG course and brain plasticity vary widely across people and over years; guidelines based on a few molecular parameters and short cognitive follow-up do not capture that longitudinal, individual trajectory.
ocar.action: Duffau, in Journal of Personalized Medicine (2022), reviews predictive tumoral and non-tumoral factors and their changing interactions to argue for a multistage, connectome-based, awake-mapping strategy tailored to each LGG patient.
ocar.resolution: He argues that early and repeat maximal connectome-based resections in awake patients can postpone malignant transformation while preserving quality of life via network reconfiguration, and that management plans should be adjusted over time rather than applying static guidelines. Mean diameter growth of about 3–4 mm per year is cited for the symptomatic slow-growth phase.
ocar.future_work: Deep-learning models are proposed to compare in silico treatment sequences for overall survival and quality of life; they are not implemented in this review.

summaries.beginner: Slow-growing brain tumors in young adults invade wiring, not just a lump. This neurosurgeon argues for planning years of surgery around each patient’s changing brain networks, instead of a one-size protocol.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Personalized Medicine (2022), Duffau reviews personalized longitudinal care for WHO grade II diffuse low-grade glioma. He describes pre-symptomatic, symptomatic (seizures/mild cognitive change; about 3–4 mm mean diameter growth per year), and malignant-transformation stages, and advocates repeat awake, connectome-based resections timed to predicted tumor kinetics and neural reorganization. Conclusions urge systematic tracking of tumor genetics, brain-reorganization, and life events, and suggest deep-learning comparisons of treatment sequences.
summaries.advanced: This is a single-author clinical review, not a trial. Growth-rate and survival numbers beyond the 3–4 mm/year citation are not tabulated in the selected extract. “Connectome-based” refers to intraoperative mapping and network plasticity, not a published patient-specific graph dataset. Deep-learning decision support is prospective.

plain_language_summary: Slow-growing brain tumors in young adults invade wiring, not just a lump. This neurosurgeon argues for planning years of surgery around each patient’s changing brain networks, instead of a one-size protocol.

ocar.opportunity: Selective vulnerability of structural networks in people at Alzheimer’s risk, before cognitive decline, could separate pathological from normal aging and open earlier intervention.
ocar.challenge: Univariate imaging-to-single-trait analyses overfit multifactorial AD risk; unsupervised PCA/ICA also ignore the risk labels one actually wants to predict.
ocar.action: Mahzarnia, Stout, Anderson, Moon, Han, Beck, Browndyke, Dunson, Johnson, O’Brien, and Badea, in Cerebral Cortex (2023; advance 2022), study 72 people across the age span enriched for APOE4, using sparse canonical correlation analysis of diffusion-MRI connectomes against composite risk (age, genotype, sex; then adding cognition), and sparse regression after extending tensor-network PCA with CCA components.
ocar.resolution: Sparse CCA put high weight on genotype, with subgraphs involving cuneus, temporal, cingulate cortices, and cerebellum. Adding cognitive metrics highlighted pericalcarine cortex, insula, banks of the superior sulcus, and cerebellum. Predictive models had errors of 17% for genotype, 24% for family risk, and 5 years for age. Age prediction that included cognitively impaired subjects revealed additional temporal, paracentral, amygdala, and parahippocampal regions not found using only normal subjects.
ocar.future_work: The authors call the work a stepping stone toward single-subject prediction and note the small number of MCI and AD participants as a limitation needing larger validation.

summaries.beginner: People who carry Alzheimer’s risk genes were scanned before most of them were ill. The study picks out brain-network patterns that track genotype, family risk, and age, aiming someday to flag individuals, not just groups.
summaries.intermediate: In Cerebral Cortex (2023), Mahzarnia, Badea and colleagues analyze diffusion connectomes from 72 people enriched for APOE4. Sparse CCA links a composite risk factor (age, genotype, sex) to subgraphs in cuneus, temporal, cingulate, and cerebellum; adding cognition highlights pericalcarine, insula, superior-sulcus banks, and cerebellum. Sparse regression errors are 17% (genotype), 24% (family risk), and 5 years (age). Impaired-inclusive age models implicate additional medial-temporal structures.
summaries.advanced: N = 72 with few MCI/AD cases is flagged by the authors. Errors are model-prediction errors, not diagnostic AUCs for incident AD. “Banks of the superior sulcus” wording follows the abstract (likely superior temporal sulcus). Single-subject clinical use is explicitly future. Overlap with the 2024 Winter/Badea mouse-risk paper is conceptual (sparse CCA), not the same dataset.

plain_language_summary: People who carry Alzheimer’s risk genes were scanned before most of them were ill. The study picks out brain-network patterns that track genotype, family risk, and age, aiming someday to flag individuals, not just groups.

ocar.opportunity: Thalamic neuromodulation is increasingly used for drug-resistant epilepsy; neuroimaging of thalamic structure, nuclei, and networks could improve targeting and outcome prediction.
ocar.challenge: The thalamus is altered in common epilepsy syndromes, traditional stereotactic coordinates may miss patient-specific nuclei, and stimulation effects on networks are incompletely characterized.
ocar.action: Middlebrooks, He, Grewal, and Keller, in Epilepsy Research (2022), as described in the catalog abstract, review neuroimaging and thalamic connectomics in epilepsy neuromodulation: thalamic changes as rationale, methods for imaging nuclei and the case for direct surgical targeting, and neuroimaging as a potential biomarker of stimulation effects and outcomes.
ocar.resolution: The review argues for imaging-defined targeting rather than reliance on traditional stereotactic coordinates alone, and for using neuroimaging to assess how thalamic stimulation alters networks and to serve as an outcome biomarker.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents these as roles neuroimaging could play; it does not report a new trial.

summaries.beginner: Stimulating the thalamus can help some people whose seizures do not respond to drugs. This review discusses how brain scans of thalamic connections might guide where to place those stimulators.
summaries.intermediate: In Epilepsy Research (2022), Middlebrooks, He, Grewal, and Keller review neuroimaging and thalamic connectomics for neuromodulation in drug-resistant epilepsy. They cover structural and functional thalamic changes as rationale, methods to image distinct nuclei and why direct targeting may beat atlas coordinates, and the potential of imaging to track stimulation effects and outcomes.
summaries.advanced: The attached PDF extract does not match this catalog record: it is Hsu, Ali, Air, Englot, Muh, Richardson, and Rammo, Thalamic neuromodulation: new frontiers (Epilepsy Currents, 2026 AES highlights), not Middlebrooks et al. 2022. Summaries here follow the Epilepsy Research abstract only. No sample sizes, seizure-reduction percentages, or named trials appear in that abstract.

plain_language_summary: Stimulating the thalamus can help some people whose seizures do not respond to drugs. This review discusses how brain scans of thalamic connections might guide where to place those stimulators.

ocar.opportunity: Olfactory loss can precede cognitive Alzheimer’s symptoms; because olfaction is conserved, mouse models plus behavior tests could support earlier detection research.
ocar.challenge: Olfactory behavior assays in AD mice are heterogeneous, often emphasize threshold and discrimination over odor memory, and may not match the tests used in patients.
ocar.action: Zhang, Zhao, Sun, Li, Wang, Dong, Yang, Lou, Yang, Li, and Li, in Brain Sciences (2022), review olfactory evaluation in AD model mice, covering traditional detection methods, cortex-involving olfactory behaviors, and published results across lines such as APP/PS1, Tg2576, 5×FAD, 3×Tg, P301S, and ApoE4.
ocar.resolution: They report that 2- to 3-month-old AD model mice can show elevated odor threshold and discrimination difficulty, paralleling early clinical olfactory loss. Studies have focused on recognition and discrimination more than odor-memory tests, which in mice have mostly been done in aged animals. Authors note experimental tweaks that increase odor types or reduce training repetitions to harden memory tests.
ocar.future_work: They call for odor-memory tests in young AD mice and for methods that better match clinical olfactory-memory assessment.

summaries.beginner: Smell often fades before memory in Alzheimer’s. This review gathers how scientists test smell in Alzheimer’s mice and what those tests have found so far.
summaries.intermediate: In Brain Sciences (2022), Zhang and colleagues review olfactory behavior assays in AD mouse models (APP/PS1, Tg2576, 5×FAD, 3×Tg, P301S, ApoE4, among those named). They emphasize threshold, discrimination, and less-studied odor memory, noting that 2- to 3-month-old AD mice can already show elevated threshold and poor discrimination. Conclusions urge odor-memory testing at young ages and harder task variants.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods-and-literature review, not new behavior data. The 2- to 3-month claim summarizes “current experimental results” without a meta-analytic table in the extract. Connectomic content is motivational (olfactory cortex) rather than a wiring-diagram result. Catalog title uses “evaluation”; the paper is behavioral, not imaging connectomics.

plain_language_summary: Smell often fades before memory in Alzheimer’s. This review gathers how scientists test smell in Alzheimer’s mice and what those tests have found so far.

ocar.opportunity: Diffuse low-grade gliomas send isolated tumor cells beyond the MRI core; defining that peritumoral zone (PTZ) as a connectome–tumor interface could improve both oncological control and function, including seizures.
ocar.challenge: Most PTZ work has been in high-grade glioma, so cellular, metabolic, and radiological features of PTZ in DLGG were under-specified, and MRI underestimates true infiltration.
ocar.action: Silva, Vivancos, and Duffau, in Brain Sciences (2022), review PTZ in DLGG and argue for connectome-guided therapy: supratotal resection that includes PTZ, sequencing of (neo)adjuvant treatments by infiltration pattern, and drugs aimed at PTZ from oncological and epileptological angles.
ocar.resolution: They report that connectome-based supratotal resection (tumor core plus PTZ) has prolonged survival by limiting malignant transformation while improving quality of life via better seizure control. They call for imaging that identifies isolated tumor cells, multimodal imaging–genetics, and PTZ-targeted immunotherapy or new AEDs.
ocar.future_work: Further multimodal PTZ investigation is presented as necessary to maximize overall survival and quality of life; new PTZ-specific drugs are proposed rather than trial-reported here.

summaries.beginner: Slow gliomas do not stop at the bright blob on the scan. This review treats the rim of mixed tumor and healthy wiring as its own zone, and argues for removing or treating that rim using brain-network maps.
summaries.intermediate: In Brain Sciences (2022), Silva, Vivancos, and Duffau review the peritumoral zone of diffuse low-grade glioma. MRI shows the dense core but misses isolated tumor cells. They advocate connectome-guided supratotal resection of core plus PTZ, citing prolonged survival, less malignant transformation, and better seizure-related quality of life, plus tailoring adjuvant therapy to infiltration pattern and developing PTZ-targeted drugs.
summaries.advanced: This is a narrative review from the Duffau group, not a randomized comparison of supratotal versus gross-total resection. Survival and seizure claims are literature-level, without new counts in the extract. PTZ remains a conceptual imaging–biology interface; radiomic/genomic markers are cited as emerging. Overlaps thematically with Duffau 2022 JPM (same shard).

plain_language_summary: Slow gliomas do not stop at the bright blob on the scan. This review treats the rim of mixed tumor and healthy wiring as its own zone, and argues for removing or treating that rim using brain-network maps.

ocar.opportunity: An open perinatal MRI resource with motion-tolerant sequences, processing derivatives, and collateral clinical and genomic data would let many groups study typical and atypical human brain development.
ocar.challenge: Fetal and neonatal imaging cannot reuse adult protocols; motion, rapid structural change, and the need for linked demographic and follow-up data have limited comparable large releases.
ocar.action: Edwards, Rueckert, Smith, Hajnal and the dHCP consortium, in Frontiers in Neuroscience (2022), describe the Developing Human Connectome Project neonatal data release: acquisition and processing protocols, available imaging and collateral data, and access routes.
ocar.resolution: The project collected 1228 multimodal MRI datasets from 1173 fetal and/or neonatal participants with collateral data. This neonatal release includes 887 datasets from 783 infants (583 healthy term-born, plus preterm and high-risk infants; many with longitudinal scans). All were studied in utero and/or soon after birth on a single scanner with novel motion-tolerant methods. Fetal data are to be released separately. Data are at developingconnectome.org and NDA collection 3955.
ocar.future_work: Discussion presents the release as an observational resource already in wide use, with companion genetic, behavioral, and atlas resources to follow from the same locations.

summaries.beginner: A large public set of baby brain scans, taken with methods that tolerate wriggling, is now available so researchers can study how human brain wiring develops around birth.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroscience (2022), Edwards, Hajnal and the dHCP consortium release neonatal data from the Developing Human Connectome Project. Across the project: 1228 multimodal MRI datasets from 1173 participants. This release: 887 datasets from 783 infants, including 583 healthy term-born plus preterm and high-risk infants, many scanned more than once, all on one scanner with motion-tolerant sequences, plus demographic, clinical, neurodevelopmental, and genomic collateral data. Fetal data are promised separately.
summaries.advanced: This is a data-descriptor paper. The abstract repeats “together with collateral… data” twice; counts used here are the stated 1228/1173 collection and 887/783 neonatal release. Image quality, yield after QC, and connectome-construction details live in processing papers/atlases, not fully in this extract. Single-scanner design reduces site effects but limits generalizability.

plain_language_summary: A large public set of baby brain scans, taken with methods that tolerate wriggling, is now available so researchers can study how human brain wiring develops around birth.

ocar.opportunity: Iba1 is the standard microglial marker; if it also functions in motility and synaptic remodeling, deleting it would test how microglia shape excitatory synapses and adult behavior.
ocar.challenge: Iba1’s functional role was unknown despite universal use as a marker, and abnormal microglia–neuron interaction is implicated in neurodevelopmental, psychiatric, and neurodegenerative disease.
ocar.action: Lituma, Woo, O’Hara, Castillo, Sibinga, and Nandi, on bioRxiv (2021), study global Aif1−/− (Iba1-deficient) mice with hippocampal slice imaging, biochemistry, neuronal labeling, whole-cell recording, engulfment assays, and adult behavior.
ocar.resolution: Juvenile Aif1−/− microglia show reduced ATP-induced motility and ramification and altered expression of pruning-associated proteins. Juvenile mutants have fewer excitatory synapses and reduced synaptic drive; synaptic engulfment capacity is unexpectedly diminished. Synapse number is already reduced in early postnatal hippocampus when formation predominates. Deficits persist into adulthood with impaired object-recognition memory and social interaction.
ocar.future_work: The significance statement suggests modifying microglial function as a therapeutic strategy; that is not tested here. The selected extract does not include a numbered results/discussion (it jumps toward methods references).

summaries.beginner: The stain everyone uses for brain immune cells turns out to matter for the cells’ job. Mice missing Iba1 have sluggish microglia, fewer excitatory synapses, and later problems with memory and social behavior.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2021), Lituma, Castillo, Sibinga, Nandi and colleagues characterize global Iba1/Aif1 knockout mice. Juvenile hippocampal microglia show reduced ATP-evoked motility and ramification; pruning-related proteins change; excitatory synapse number and transmission fall; engulfment is reduced rather than increased. Early postnatal synapse counts are already low. Adults show impaired novel-object recognition and social interaction. Catalog journal lists PNAS; the extract is the 23 April 2021 preprint.
summaries.advanced: The attached extract is the matching Lituma et al. preprint but is thin after the abstract (methods references, not a full discussion). No numeric synapse counts, mEPSC frequencies, or behavior scores appear in the selected text. The knockout is global, so non-microglial Aif1 contributions are not excluded by this design as described. Catalog UUID/DOI is the bioRxiv identifier.

plain_language_summary: The stain everyone uses for brain immune cells turns out to matter for the cells’ job. Mice missing Iba1 have sluggish microglia, fewer excitatory synapses, and later problems with memory and social behavior.

ocar.opportunity: Open multimodal MRI with aligned microstructure, tractography, functional connectivity, and geodesic-distance connectomes plus gradients would let others test how cortical wiring couples to myelin architecture.
ocar.challenge: Investigating large-scale gradients in microstructure and connectivity requires multiple contrasts, many parcellation scales, and reproducible derivatives, which few shared datasets provide together.
ocar.action: Royer, Rodríguez-Cruces, Tavakol, Larivière, Herholz, Li, Vos de Wael, Paquola, Benkarim, Park, Lowe, Margulies, Smallwood, Bernasconi, Bernasconi, Frauscher, and Bernhardt, in Scientific Data (2022), release MICA-MICs: multimodal MRI in 50 healthy adults with raw data plus connectomes and gradients across parcellations, processed with micapipe.
ocar.resolution: Fifty healthy adults (23 women; 29.54 ± 5.62 years) were scanned at 3 T with high-resolution T1w, myelin-sensitive quantitative T1, diffusion MRI, and resting-state fMRI. Derivatives include functional, diffusion-tractography, microstructure-covariance, and geodesic-distance connectomes plus gradients at multiple scales. Data are on CONP and OSF; code at GitHub MICA-MNI/micapipe.
ocar.future_work: The descriptor aims to facilitate research on microstructure–connectivity–function coupling; no new biological result is claimed beyond the resource.

summaries.beginner: A public MRI collection gives both the raw scans and ready-made brain-network matrices from several types of images, so other labs can ask how tissue structure lines up with wiring and activity.
summaries.intermediate: In Scientific Data (2022), Royer, Bernhardt and colleagues release MICA-MICs from 50 healthy adults (23 women; mean age 29.54 ± 5.62 years) scanned at 3 T (T1w, qT1, DWI, rs-fMRI). Besides anonymized raw data they share functional, structural, microstructure-covariance, and geodesic-distance connectomes and gradients at multiple parcellations, with usage notes on matrix ordering (including medial wall and subcortex). Hosted on CONP and OSF; pipeline is micapipe.
summaries.advanced: This is a data descriptor for healthy adults only. Mean age ± SD is given; other demographics are not in the selected extract. Catalog year is 2021 (bioRxiv) while the extract is the 2022 Scientific Data version—same study. Connectomes are MRI-derived, not tracer- or EM-verified.

plain_language_summary: A public MRI collection gives both the raw scans and ready-made brain-network matrices from several types of images, so other labs can ask how tissue structure lines up with wiring and activity.

ocar.opportunity: Deep brain stimulation can help severe obsessive-compulsive disorder, but connecting stimulation sites to distributed networks rather than a single nucleus could explain clinical benefit and unify cortical and subcortical interventions.
ocar.challenge: Best anatomical targets and mechanisms remain ambiguous, limiting routine clinical use even when DBS is considered effective.
ocar.action: Baldermann, Schüller, Kohl, Voon, Li, Hollunder, Figee, Haber, Sheth, Mosley, Huys, Johnson, Butson, Ackermans, Bouwens van der Vlis, Leentjens, Barbe, Visser-Vandewalle, Kuhn, and Horn, in Biological Psychiatry (2021), as described in the catalog abstract, critically review connectomic DBS for OCD, integrating connectivity analyses with neuromodulation to characterize a network whose modulation reduces obsessions and compulsions.
ocar.resolution: They argue that broader network changes, not only local impact at the electrode, account for improvement, scrutinize conflicting findings to merge common and diverse pathways, and propose a unified network that, when modulated cortically or subcortically, alleviates OCD symptoms.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents a synthesized target network rather than a prospective trial of that map.

summaries.beginner: Brain stimulation for severe OCD may work by hitting a whole circuit, not one tiny spot. This review tries to draw that circuit from imaging and stimulation studies.
summaries.intermediate: In Biological Psychiatry (2021), Baldermann, Horn and colleagues review connectomic deep brain stimulation for obsessive-compulsive disorder. They argue that distributed network effects better explain symptom relief than local stimulation alone, reconcile apparently conflicting target findings, and propose a unified network for cortical or subcortical neuromodulation.
summaries.advanced: The attached PDF extract does not match this catalog record: it is González, Rumià, Brell and colleagues, From lobotomy to connectomics: a critical review of contemporary psychosurgery (Frontiers in Psychiatry, 2026), not Baldermann et al. 2021 on OCD DBS. Summaries here follow the Biological Psychiatry abstract only. No electrode coordinates, tractography atlases, or outcome percentages appear in that abstract.

plain_language_summary: Brain stimulation for severe OCD may work by hitting a whole circuit, not one tiny spot. This review tries to draw that circuit from imaging and stimulation studies.

ocar.opportunity: Undergraduate neuroscience majors who can handle data-science and graph-theoretic tools would be able to read contemporary systems and connectomics literature rather than remaining on a calculus-plus-parametric-statistics diet.
ocar.challenge: Credit-hour pressure, outdated statistics requirements, and faculty whose quantitative skills have atrophied leave students ill-equipped for big-data neuroscience, including connectomics framed as 21st-century functional neuroanatomy.
ocar.action: Hoy, in Neuroscience Letters (2021), as described in the catalog abstract, comments on quantitative skills in undergraduate neuroscience education, arguing for data-science coursework of the kind required in social sciences and for short-format workshops, journal clubs, and independent studies in which students and instructors learn together, using neuroscience-contextualized materials.
ocar.resolution: The commentary holds that additional training in mathematics, statistics, computer science, and/or data science is urgently needed even to understand current literature, and that faculty awareness of the gap can be ameliorated (not solved) by co-learning formats and web teaching clips.
ocar.future_work: Curriculum reform at scale is urged; the piece does not report an implemented course evaluation.

summaries.beginner: Neuroscience students still take old-style math while the field now runs on huge datasets and network graphs. This commentary says they need data-science training, even if faculty have to learn alongside them.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuroscience Letters (2021), R. Hoy comments that the traditional year of calculus plus a semester of parametric statistics does not prepare undergraduate neuroscience majors for big-data and systems work, including connectomics. Students are credit-squeezed; faculty may feel their quantitative skills have faded. Hoy recommends data-science courses used in social sciences and co-learning workshops/journal clubs with neuroscience-contextualized quantitative teaching.
summaries.advanced: The attached PDF extract does not match this catalog record: it is Truong, Moore, Ricoy, and Verpeut, Low-cost approaches in neuroscience to teach machine learning using a cockroach model (eNeuro, 2024), not Hoy 2021. Summaries here follow the Neuroscience Letters abstract only. No enrollment statistics or controlled education outcomes appear in that abstract. (The mismatched paper does cite Hoy 2021 in its introduction.)

plain_language_summary: Neuroscience students still take old-style math while the field now runs on huge datasets and network graphs. This commentary says they need data-science training, even if faculty have to learn alongside them.

ocar.opportunity: BRAIN Initiative technologies will change circuit science only if they are validated, disseminated, and integrated into usable community systems spanning subcellular labels to brain-wide networks.
ocar.challenge: Innovators, funders, and non-federal partners lacked a shared playbook for turning promising tools into mature, accessible resources; scientific impact depends on adoption, not only invention.
ocar.action: Litvina, Adams, Barth, Bruchez, Carson, Chung, Dupre, Frank, Gates, Harris, Joo, Lichtman, Ramos, Sejnowski, Trimmer, White, and Koroshetz, in Journal of Neuroscience (2019), describe early dissemination strategies and spotlight Mini-Symposium teams providing EM- and fluorescence-based connectomics systems, immunolabeling advances, and tools for recording and analyzing functional connectivity.
ocar.resolution: The mini-symposium paper catalogs community-facing resources and argues that continued investment in access, training, data sharing, diversity, and neuroethics is required for BRAIN tools to yield insight into healthy and disordered brain circuits.
ocar.future_work: The piece is an invitation to dialogue and a snapshot of 2019 resources, not a quantitative adoption study.

summaries.beginner: Inventing a new brain tool is not enough; people have to be able to get it and use it. This BRAIN Initiative mini-symposium paper showcases projects that are trying to share connectomics and recording methods with the wider community.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Neuroscience (2019), Litvina, Koroshetz and colleagues outline NIH BRAIN Initiative dissemination strategy and highlight investigator teams offering integrated EM- and fluorescence-based connectomics, immunolabeling, and functional-connectivity recording/analysis resources. The accompanying SfN Mini-Symposium is the public face of those tools. Closing arguments emphasize training, collaboration, data sharing, diversity, and neuroethics.
summaries.advanced: This is a program/mini-symposium overview, not a methods benchmark. Individual tool performance lives in the cited primary papers (e.g., Lichtman EM systems, Harris immunolabeling). “Florescence-based” is the extract’s spelling for fluorescence. Year six of BRAIN funding is stated as context.

plain_language_summary: Inventing a new brain tool is not enough; people have to be able to get it and use it. This BRAIN Initiative mini-symposium paper showcases projects that are trying to share connectomics and recording methods with the wider community.

ocar.opportunity: An anatomically grounded 3D atlas of human axonal pathways would give education, science, and DBS planning a reference that tractography alone cannot provide.
ocar.challenge: Diffusion tractography is indirect and limited, and no single neuroanatomist holds pathway knowledge across cortex, basal ganglia, and cerebellum in a common human coordinate system.
ocar.action: Petersen, Mlakar, Haber, Parent, Smith, Strick, Griswold, and McIntyre, in Neuron (2019), built a holographic interface populated with human histology and structural MRI, then had expert neuroanatomists interactively define trajectories of cortical, basal ganglia, and cerebellar systems, with emphasis on the subthalamic region relevant to Parkinson DBS.
ocar.resolution: They present what they describe as the first holographic pathway-building interface and an anatomist-defined human axonal atlas that integrates decades of knowledge. Discussion contrasts the atlas with HCP-style group connectomes used for STN DBS (Horn et al., 2019) and reports substantial discrepancies, positioning the atlas as an independent test case for tractography.
ocar.future_work: They propose repeating the holographic group-expertise framework elsewhere in the brain to generate anatomical priors for human connectomic analyses.

summaries.beginner: Instead of trusting computer-drawn water-diffusion “wires,” expert anatomists stood in a hologram of the human brain and drew the real axonal paths, especially around a deep target used for Parkinson’s stimulation.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron (2019), Petersen, McIntyre and colleagues created a holographic workspace combining human histology and structural MRI so expert neuroanatomists could jointly trace cortical, basal ganglia, and cerebellar axons. They frame this as overcoming tractography’s limits and meeting a clinical need for a subthalamic pathway atlas for DBS. Discussion compares anatomist-defined paths to a group connectome used for STN DBS and notes substantial discrepancies.
summaries.advanced: “First holographic interface” is an authorship claim. Pathway trajectories are expert consensus on integrated data, not new tracer experiments in human. Discrepancies with tractography are described qualitatively in this extract (Figure 6 is cited, not numerically summarized). Generalization beyond the subthalamic test case is proposed.

plain_language_summary: Instead of trusting computer-drawn water-diffusion “wires,” expert anatomists stood in a hologram of the human brain and drew the real axonal paths, especially around a deep target used for Parkinson’s stimulation.

ocar.opportunity: Birds achieve complex cognition without a six-layered cortex; comparing hippocampal connectivity and adult neurogenesis along the anterior–posterior axis could inform hippocampal evolution.
ocar.challenge: Early comparative anatomy misread the avian telencephalon as a hypertrophied striatum; even with a pallial consensus, species-specific hippocampal morphology still complicates homology with mammals.
ocar.action: Herold, Schlömer, Mafoppa-Fomat, Mehlhorn, Amunts, and Axer, in Cortex (2019), as described in the catalog abstract, use 3D polarized light imaging (3D-PLI) on the pigeon hippocampal formation (HF) and assess adult neurogenesis across HF subdivisions and caudal regions.
ocar.resolution: Pigeon HF, like mammalian HF, shows regional specializations of connectivity along the anterior–posterior axis, plus different levels of adult neurogenesis in subdivisions and in the most caudal regions, pointing to functional specialization along that axis. The authors conclude that morphologies are species-specific but hippocampal characteristics of connectivity, cells, and adult neurogenesis remain conserved relative to mammals.
ocar.future_work: The abstract offers new aspects for ongoing debates on hippocampal evolution and mind, without claiming a completed homology table.

summaries.beginner: Bird brains do not look like mammal brains, but their hippocampus still has specialized wiring along its length. This pigeon imaging study adds that pattern to the evolutionary comparison.
summaries.intermediate: In Cortex (2019), Herold, Amunts, Axer and colleagues apply 3D polarized light imaging to pigeon hippocampal formation and report anterior–posterior specialization of connectivity, together with subdivision- and caudal-dependent adult neurogenesis. They argue for conserved hippocampal traits of connectivity, cells, and neurogenesis despite species-specific morphology.
summaries.advanced: The attached PDF extract does not match this catalog record: it is Fujita, Aoki, Mori, Homma, and Yamaguchi, Homologous cell type markers highlight subdivisions of the domestic chick hippocampal formation (Scientific Reports), not Herold et al. 2019 on pigeon 3D-PLI. Summaries here follow the Cortex abstract only. No 3D-PLI anisotropy values or neurogenesis cell counts appear in that abstract.

plain_language_summary: Bird brains do not look like mammal brains, but their hippocampus still has specialized wiring along its length. This pigeon imaging study adds that pattern to the evolutionary comparison.

ocar.opportunity: A focused comparison of primate connectomes, rather than all animals at once, could show which long-range connections are shared and which are human- or species-specific adaptations.
ocar.challenge: Long-range connections improve communication but are costly; methods (white-matter volume, histology, tracers, dMRI tractography, functional MRI) disagree, and cortical homologies plus false-positive tractography remain obstacles.
ocar.action: Rilling and van den Heuvel, in Brain, Behavior and Evolution (2018), as described in the catalog abstract, review comparative primate connectomics across structural and resting-state measures, including humans, chimpanzees, and rhesus macaques, and outline how to expand species coverage with postmortem diffusion tractography.
ocar.resolution: Larger primate brains appear less well connected globally than smaller ones, yet humans have more connections than expected for cortical neuron number, possibly concentrated in prefrontal cortex. Human-specific structural and functional connections are reported in language, imitation, tool-use, and (for functional connectivity) empathy-related cortex, against a background of widespread overlap with nonhuman primates. Comparative work can also detect specializations in non-human species.
ocar.future_work: They urge postmortem dMRI to include more species, careful homology, better tractography to limit false positives/negatives, and linking connectivity variation to behavior within and across species.

summaries.beginner: This review compares wiring maps among primates and asks what is unusual about human long-range connections, especially in language and tool-use areas.
summaries.intermediate: In Brain, Behavior and Evolution (2018), Rilling and van den Heuvel review comparative primate connectomics. They synthesize white-matter, tracing, dMRI, and functional-connectivity evidence: larger primate brains are less globally connected, but humans may exceed expectations given cortical neuron number (possibly prefrontal). Overlap with macaques/chimpanzees is broad, with human-specific links in language, imitation, tool use, and empathy-related functional connections. They recommend expanding postmortem tractography beyond the usual three species.
summaries.advanced: The attached PDF extract does not match this catalog record: it is Henningsen-Schomers and Pulvermüller, Modelling concrete and abstract concepts using brain-constrained deep neural networks (Psychological Research, 2022), not Rilling and van den Heuvel 2018. Summaries here follow the Brain, Behavior and Evolution abstract only. No quantitative edge-overlap percentages or tractography error rates appear in that abstract.

plain_language_summary: This review compares wiring maps among primates and asks what is unusual about human long-range connections, especially in language and tool-use areas.

ocar.opportunity: If autism involves long-range underconnectivity, electron-microscopic morphometry of anatomically distinct corpus callosum segments could supply cellular markers of distorted interhemispheric connectome integrity.
ocar.challenge: MRI supports disconnection theories but does not resolve axon number, diameter, and segment-specific specialization in the callosum.
ocar.action: Wegiel, Kaczmarski, Flory, Martínez-Cerdeño, Wisniewski, Nowicki, Kuchna, and Wegiel, in Acta Neuropathologica Communications (2018), perform EM morphometry of five CC segments in nine neurotypical and nine autistic subjects.
ocar.resolution: Average axon diameter and cross-sectional area were reduced in autism, with less segment-specific diversification. The percentage of small-diameter axons (<0.651 μm) increased and large-diameter axons (>1.051 μm) decreased. Total small-diameter axons were reduced in segments I and III by 43% on average; medium- and large-diameter axons were reduced in all five segments by an average of 49% and 72%, respectively. The authors interpret guidance and axon-structure control failures, with likely effects on conduction velocity and functional specialization.
ocar.future_work: Conclusions generalize to loss of higher-order and multisensory integration capacity; behavioral correlation in this sample is not developed in the selected extract.

summaries.beginner: The big cable between the two halves of the brain has fewer and thinner axons in the autistic cases studied here, especially the large, fast-conducting fibers.
summaries.intermediate: In Acta Neuropathologica Communications (2018), Wegiel and colleagues compare five corpus callosum segments in nine autistic and nine neurotypical brains with electron microscopy. Mean axon diameter and area fall; small axons (<0.651 μm) become a larger percentage and large axons (>1.051 μm) a smaller one. Counts: small-diameter axons down 43% on average in segments I and III; medium- and large-diameter axons down 49% and 72% on average across all five segments. They frame this as developmental guidance and structural failure contributing to connectome-integrity distortion.
summaries.advanced: N = 9 per group is small for a heterogeneous clinical category. Postmortem EM morphometry does not measure functional connectivity. Percent changes are group averages as stated; individual-level scatter is not in the extract. Causal links to the autism behavioral phenotype are interpretive. Catalog method tag correctly includes electron microscopy.

plain_language_summary: The big cable between the two halves of the brain has fewer and thinner axons in the autistic cases studied here, especially the large, fast-conducting fibers.

ocar.opportunity: Structural and physiological neuroimaging of fetuses and infants could reveal how transient compartments, axons, synapses, and functional networks assemble—and eventually support early intervention—if adult imaging concepts are replaced by development-specific biology.
ocar.challenge: Rapid change, unique fetal compartments, immature neurovascular coupling, and technical limits of MRI, EEG, MEG, and NIRS mean adult pipelines cannot be transferred, and modulators such as the placenta are often ignored.
ocar.action: Vasung, Turk, Ferradal, Sutin, Stout, Ahtam, Lin, and Grant, in NeuroImage (2019; 2018 online), review early human brain development: transient structures and axonal connectivity (ex vivo/in vivo MRI), synaptic circuitry, neurovascular coupling and metabolism, functional connectivity, complementary physiological methods, and emerging placental MRI, with technical and biological limitations in each section.
ocar.resolution: They summarize that cortex matures from primary to association areas and that limbic and projection pathways precede association pathways. From 15 gestational weeks the telencephalon comprises six transient compartments plus ganglionic eminence. Histology remains irreplaceable while MRI/DTI characterize spatio-temporal change. The review stresses a dire need for technical innovation to enable fetal and infant interventions that avert long-term disease.
ocar.future_work: Placental MRI and better physiological–structural integration are highlighted as incomplete; the paper is a synthesis, not a new cohort.

summaries.beginner: A baby’s brain is not a miniature adult brain. This review explains what MRI and related tools can and cannot show about how human brain structure and function grow before and just after birth.
summaries.intermediate: In NeuroImage (2019), Vasung, Grant and colleagues review structural and physiological neuroimaging from embryo to infancy. They cover transient fetal compartments, axonal then synaptic connectivity, neurovascular coupling, metabolism, fMRI functional connectivity, and EEG/MEG/NIRS, plus placental modulators. MRI/DTI contributions are set against histology as gold standard. Cited organizational facts include six transient telencephalic compartments from 15 gestational weeks and primary-to-association cortical and pathway maturation sequences.
summaries.advanced: This is a wide-ranging review. Many biological claims are cited from the histological canon (Kostović, Rakic, etc.), not newly measured here. Adult-to-infant transfer of fMRI connectivity interpretations is explicitly cautioned. No single quantitative developmental curve is the paper’s result. Catalog year 2018 matches online availability.

plain_language_summary: A baby’s brain is not a miniature adult brain. This review explains what MRI and related tools can and cannot show about how human brain structure and function grow before and just after birth.

ocar.opportunity: Relating DBS electrode location to clinical outcome and to structural/functional networks requires a shared, updatable open pipeline rather than one-off reconstructions.
ocar.challenge: Since Lead-DBS launched in 2014, registration, brain-shift correction, segmented-lead orientation, microelectrode recordings, volume-of-tissue-activated models, and connectomic analyses proliferated and needed a revised end-to-end workflow usable in both high-field research and routine 1.5 T clinics.
ocar.action: Horn, Li, Dembek, Kappel, Boulay, Ewert, Tietze, Husch, Perera, Neumann, Reisert, Si, Oostenveld, Rorden, Yeh, Fang, Herrington, Vorwerk, and Kühn, in NeuroImage (2019), present Lead-DBS v2, demonstrating updated DBS and connectome pipelines on a 3 T example patient (comparing multiple co-registration, warping, electrode, VTA, tractography, and connectivity methods) and on a retrospective cohort of 51 Parkinson patients scanned at 1.5 T, relating model choices to variance in clinical improvement.
ocar.resolution: The paper is framed as a multi-institutional comprehensive open-source pipeline for DBS imaging and connectomics that had already empowered several studies. Limitations-and-future-directions break the stack into anatomy, stimulation-effect (E-field/VTA), and further layers, noting strong dependence on imaging quality, trade-offs of postoperative CT versus MRI, and the need for histology-informed atlases and methods such as polarized light imaging.
ocar.future_work: Each modeling layer is described as improvable with better MRI (including QSM and ultra-high-field), conductivity-informed VTA, and extra-MRI anatomy sources.

summaries.beginner: To know whether a deep-brain stimulator is in the right spot, and which networks it is ticking, labs need shared software. This paper updates the open Lead-DBS toolbox to a full imaging-and-connectome pipeline.
summaries.intermediate: In NeuroImage (2019), Horn, Kühn and colleagues describe Lead-DBS v2: nonlinear multispectral registration, connectivity analyses, brain-shift correction, microelectrode-recording reconstruction, and segmented-lead orientation. They demo a 3 T patient (five co-registration algorithms, ten warps, three electrode methods, four VTA models, four tractography algorithms, eight connectivity approaches) and a 51-patient 1.5 T Parkinson cohort, comparing how preprocessing choices affect explained variance in clinical improvement.
summaries.advanced: The extract’s abstract lists the combinatorial method comparisons; per-algorithm winners and exact R² values are not in the selected text. Catalog journal field says bioRxiv; the extract is the NeuroImage author manuscript. Clinical-improvement variance is the evaluation target, not a claim of a single best atlas. DBS connectomes here are MRI tractography/functional maps around stimulation volumes.

plain_language_summary: To know whether a deep-brain stimulator is in the right spot, and which networks it is ticking, labs need shared software. This paper updates the open Lead-DBS toolbox to a full imaging-and-connectome pipeline.

ocar.opportunity: Most schizophrenia risk variants lie in noncoding regulatory sequence; mapping how chromosomal looping in developing neural cells links those variants to distant genes would expand the disease gene network in a cell-type-specific way.
ocar.challenge: The brain’s three-dimensional genome, including developmental and cell-type regulation of TADs and loops at SZ loci, was poorly understood.
ocar.action: Rajarajan, Borrman, Liao, Schrode, Flaherty, Casiño, Powell, Yashaswini, LaMarca, Kassim, Javidfar, Espeso-Gil, Li, Won, Geschwind, Ho, MacDonald, Hoffman, Roussos, Zhang, Hahn, Weng, Brennand, and Akbarian, in Science (2018), use Hi-C on isogenic iPSC-derived neural progenitors differentiating into neurons or astrocyte-like glia, mapping loops anchored in common SZ variant sequences.
ocar.resolution: Differentiation remodels 3D genome structure (pruning and de novo loops). Neurons and NPCs harbor more SZ-risk-anchored interactions than glia. Risk-locus-connect genes expand known GWAS overlap by about 50–150% depending on cell type (NPC: 386 genes, 146 in loci + 240 distal; neuron: 385 = 158 + 227; glia: 201 = 88 + 113). The chromosomal connectome shows coordinated transcription and protein interactions, with clusters enriched for neuronal connectivity/synaptic plasticity and for chromatin regulators. Developmentally regulated conformation changes at SZ sequences occurred disproportionately in neurons.
ocar.future_work: CRISPR functional validation is cited in the graphical summary; the selected extract is mostly the structured abstract and author list, without the full discussion.

summaries.beginner: Schizophrenia risk DNA often sits far from the genes it may control. By folding maps of chromosomes in developing human brain cells, this study finds extra genes that physically touch those risk regions, especially in neurons.
summaries.intermediate: In Science (2018), Rajarajan, Brennand, Akbarian and colleagues map Hi-C chromosomal contacts during iPSC neural progenitor differentiation into neurons or glia. SZ common-variant sequences participate in cell-type-specific loops that add distal “risk locus–connect” genes (NPC 240, neuron 227, glia 113) to in-locus genes, expanding the network by about 50–150%. Neuronal ensembles are enriched for connectivity/plasticity and chromatin regulators, and 3D-genome remodeling at risk sites is neuron-biased.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF text is short and is dominated by the structured abstract plus author contributions; results figures and CRISPR details are not in the extract. Gene counts are those stated in the abstract. This is an in vitro iPSC model, not a postmortem brain Hi-C atlas. “Chromosomal connectome” is spatial genome proximity, not synaptic wiring.

plain_language_summary: Schizophrenia risk DNA often sits far from the genes it may control. By folding maps of chromosomes in developing human brain cells, this study finds extra genes that physically touch those risk regions, especially in neurons.
